svg.aria-label: Diagram: AWS Nitro Sandboxes give each EKS pod, ECS task or lightweight VM its own hardware-isolated child virtual machine on a shared EC2 instance, with its own Linux kernel, isolated from the parent instance, from other sandboxes and from AWS operators, at no additional charge. The isolation is precisely scoped. Memory is isolated in confidential mode, where it is moved out of the parent instance so the parent cannot read it. CPU is isolated as a security boundary, which EKS states is not a performance reservation. The kernel is isolated and shares no kernel or memory mappings with the parent or other sandboxes. But the parent instance's network stack is a shared per-instance resource, and so is the instance's overall device limit. AWS states that a single Nitro Sandbox can exhaust parent-side resources such as the connection-tracking table or the DNS resolver budget and deny network access to other Nitro Sandboxes on the same instance, and that as the parent operator you must cap or rate-limit these resources for each sandbox. So the threat model holds for confidentiality and integrity but not for availability between tenants. Two modes set the trust direction: confidential mode is the default, moves memory beyond the parent and provides attestation, while direct mode shares memory with the parent, has no attestation and a trust model equivalent to a standard nested virtual machine. Confidential mode's guarantee is incomplete without action, because without a KMS key policy or equivalent external verifier checking PCR values the attestation measurement is recorded but never verified. Capacity is bounded despite being free: total vCPUs across all sandboxes on an instance cannot exceed five times the instance vCPU count, so a 4-vCPU instance has a 20 vCPU budget, which is ten sandboxes at two vCPUs each, and each sandbox's memory is donated in full at start, stays reserved until termination and is not overcommitted, so memory usually sets density. vCPU and memory cannot be changed during a sandbox's life. Availability has three different answers: the announcement says most Nitro-based EC2 instances in all commercial regions worldwide, the EC2 primitive requires an instance type that supports Nitro Enclaves, and the EKS isolated and confidential pods integration is available only in US commercial AWS Regions and requires Kubernetes 1.36 or later. GPU passthrough is currently unavailable.
svg.title: Hardware-isolated, with the network stack shared
svg.text: Compute and memory are isolated. The network stack is not.
“The Nitro System isolates the compute and memory of each Nitro Sandbox, but the parent instance’s network
stack is a shared, per-instance resource.”
What the boundary covers
memory isolated — in confidential mode, moved beyond the parent’s reach
kernel isolated — “its own Linux kernel”, shared with nothing
CPU a security boundary, “not a performance reservation” (EKS)
network stack SHARED, per instance | device limit SHARED, per instance
Holds for confidentiality and integrity. Does not hold for availability between tenants.
The exhaustion path, named in the docs
“A single Nitro Sandbox can exhaust parent-side resources, such as the connection-tracking (conntrack) table
or the DNS resolver budget, and deny network access to other Nitro Sandboxes on the same instance.”
“As the parent operator, cap or rate-limit these resources for each Nitro Sandbox.” — the mitigation is yours.
Two modes, two trust directions
confidential (default) memory beyond the parent,
plus attestation.
direct parent keeps memory access, no
attestation — “equivalent to a nested VM”.
Attestation is recorded, not checked
“Without a KMS key policy … that checks PCR
values, the attestation measurement is recorded
but never verified, and the confidentiality
guarantees … are incomplete.”
Free of charge, bounded in capacity
vCPU budget 5 x the instance’s vCPU count — a 4-vCPU instance gets 20 vCPUs,
which is 10 sandboxes at 2 vCPUs each; larger means fewer
Memory is donated in full at start and not overcommitted, so memory, not vCPU, usually sets density.
“All commercial regions worldwide” is the EC2 primitive. The integrations are narrower.
EC2 needs an instance type that supports Nitro Enclaves
EKS US commercial Regions only, Kubernetes 1.36+ | GPU passthrough: unavailable
A VM boundary at container density for no extra charge — priced in dedicated memory, and in a network stack you must cap yourself.
